utterances.text: And those corrections were because there were some things in the original statement that were not true. Is that not right? Perhaps mistakes made by whoever wrote it down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe. I have no idea. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, if you said in that statement that the room was 3.2 metres by 2.2 meet metres back in 1994, would that have been right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember what I said. This was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, would it help you to see a copy of that statement? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think she has said precisely the same thing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. That room had two doors in it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the doors was always blocked. You could not use it. Is that not right and the other --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other door, the door that you went through, what kind of door was that? Was it a solid door like we have on the edge of the court room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A wooden door, an ordinary door. How do I know?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean, was it a door that you could see through when it was closed? Excuse me one second, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just been told that the interpreters are having a hard time hearing me. Could I use the podium? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour: I think this may be a little bit better. Is it? Okay. Thank you. Ma'am, when you were being held in in that room, was the door generally kept open or kept closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Closed. I could just see through the -- the gates through the window then, when the door was closed, and when I went out, I could see more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, the door was generally closed, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would always close it behind me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the guards would keep it closed also, would they not, because you were a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When the guards would come in, when they raped me, they would close the door. They would also use the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, but the toilet that the guards used was at a different place than the room you were kept in, was it not, a different place in the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they -- at night they would use our toilet and they held the keys, and they would lock us up from the outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the day did they keep you locked up from the outside also in the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The main entrance was always locked, but when we had to sweep outside, then they had to unlock it and open the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were sweeping outside generally how much time would you be outside? Would it be half an hour or an hour or two hours? A long time or a short time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends. Sometimes you would sweep the road. There was a tree. The leaves would be falling down. Sometimes it took longer; sometimes shorter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time-frame are we talking about? Are we talking generally about half an hour or generally about an hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't watch the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you did not even have a watch, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, when you were taken prisoner and arrested, all of your personal property was taken from you, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything was set alight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pardon me, ma'am? I did not understand you. Everything was what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They set fire to my house, what was left. They couldn't burn the land. They would have if they could, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, but when you were arrested you had some things with you. You hid your wedding ring, but perhaps some other jewellery, other things. When you were taken prisoner, the people who arrested you and the people who put you in the camp took all of the property you had with you away from you, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Ibrahim Duro took my money because he said to me: "If you don't give it to me, they'll take it anyway", and I gave it to him. I took off my ring and I left it at my brother-in-law's house. The rest was in my handbag with my personal ID card and some medicines that I had on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the camp, the guards let you keep that, or did they take it away from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I kept it. They didn't take it away from me, because they searched us. They searched me near my house. They saw there was nothing inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you said in the corrections you made to your statement that you gave to the court in Yugoslavia, the corrections that we were provided with by the prosecution today, that you had five packets of contraceptive pills when you went to Celebici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the way that the investigating magistrate originally wrote his report, he said -- typed -- you had gotten them just before the attack by the Muslim Croat army and you correct that to say "quite a long time before the attack". Which is right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I bought them on 1st April 1992, because medicines were already in short supply. I found the pills and I bought myself this quantity, and I used them while I was living with my husband.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did your doctor prescribe them for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for several years I had been using them in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your doctor's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. It was a woman doctor anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would Dr Sayed, and I will spell the last name for you, J-U-S-U-F-B-E-G-O-V-I-C, would that be your doctor's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe it was Sejo, but I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, ma'am, you were taking those pills since, what, January of 1986, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't remember the date, but it's a fact I'd used them for a long time. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you used up the prescription in April of 1991, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got it without a prescription. You were able to buy them without any prescriptions in private pharmacies. There was a pharmacy near the bridge next to the bank on the right-hand side as I walked up from my house, and I dropped by the pharmacy and bought them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, at the end of March in 1992 you had gotten pregnant, had you not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour, as to relevancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may continue, I think I can tie it up. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think I sustain the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would it surprise you if Dr Sayed -- and I cannot pronounce his last name; I apologise -- told our investigator that he last saw you on April 1st, 1992 and did not prescribe any contraceptive pills?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I object and explain why I object? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: What is your objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection would be two-fold. The first is, given that the witness has already just, I believe, stated that she did not get them with a prescription, I believe this is irrelevant, but it goes to a broader issue, which was raised yesterday, and I would like to explain to the court why I object. I believe it is improper for defence counsel to ask a witness whether or not they would be surprised at what another witness may or may not say. I do not believe that the defence may I impeach a witness by reporting what other persons may or may not have said. The prosecution certainly believes that they may lay the foundation for impeachment by asking the witness about certain facts and then later on in their case bringing in witnesses or documents which will support the impeachment. For instance, if the defence wishes to ask Mrs Cecez: "Did you or did you not receive a prescription from your doctor in April of 1992?", I believe they have may do that. If they are then able to at some later point bring in what the doctor or the documents say, that is proper, but I do not believe -- or if somehow this witness can authenticate the records, or if it is the witness's own statement, but the witness's opinion about what other persons may have said or may not have said is irrelevant. This witness has no way of knowing what other people may have said, and the opinion as to whether or not it is a surprise or not a surprise is entirely irrelevant to the truth-finding process. I particularly bring this up because I think there are maybe situations where the other evidence, for instance, may be unreliable. It could be that another person was forced or coerced. It could be that another person is mistaken, and it could be that the other person is intentionally not telling the truth, but it is improper and unfair to the witness, and I believe misleading to this court to somehow ask the witness their own opinion about what other people may have said. So if the defence wishes to impeach this witness with her own prior statement, we have no objection. If the defence wishes to bring in evidence in its case which contradicts facts of this witness, we do not object. If the defence in closing argument wants to point out contradictions, we do not object, but we do object to asking a witness about what other persons have said and would they be surprised, and what is their opinion. We believe that it is a back door way of getting in evidence that may or may not be admissible and may or may not be reliable. In particular, I will talk about something that happened yesterday. Much of what happened yesterday had to do with approximately 100 -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually I am not sure you are talking about the same things.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr Moran -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: What is the question he is asking? Have you got the question he asked?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: "Would you be surprised if a doctor said ..." JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: "Your doctor", not "a doctor".

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: "Would you be surprised if your doctor said that X?" JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I breach the witness's opinion as to whether or not she would be surprised or not surprised is entirely irrelevant. I certainly believe the defence is entitled to say: "In April of 1992, did you or did you not have a prescription?" JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think she can answer the question. It is a simple and straightforward question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Ma'am, would you like me to repeat the question? Do you need me to repeat it? Ma'am, would it surprise you if your doctor said that you came to him around the end of April -- excuse me -- the beginning of April or late March in 1992 and that at that time he did not prescribe any contraceptive pills for you, and, in fact, he told you that because of your age he would recommend a different type of contraceptive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was pregnant that year and I didn't have enough of those medicines, so that I didn't use them for a time, and indeed I became pregnant. I think his name was Sejo. I went for a check-up. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) I came to Sejo. He was going to send me to Sarajevo but the situation there was already tense. I didn't dare to go. Then he told me to come and I think (redacted). Then I came back and I found those pills and bought five little boxes in this pharmacy, and I continued using them. That is true. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted). My question was whether you would be surprised if --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know what happened to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, your doctor told you it would be better to use some other kind of contraceptive form because of your age; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't say anything at the time. (redacted) (redacted). I came back home. I rested for a day or two and then I continued working. Maybe he said something, but I really don't remember, but it is a fact that I used those pills from before, and they could be purchased without a prescription.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you gave some of those pills to Milojka Antic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, she didn't use them. Only the women from Bradina used them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So she received none of those pills?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have just a second? Ma'am, have you made some appearances on television perhaps in Serbia to talk about what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have a TV set, so I have no idea. Nor do I have a TV set now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you ever meet with any people with TV cameras, who interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea. Maybe I did. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just don't remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Ma'am, in any of the statements you gave before today did you ever mention the incident with the machine gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't remember it. I recalled it this time just now. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, the question was did you, prior to today, in any of the statements you gave mention that machine gun incident?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object that it has been asked and answered. She already stated she does not remember. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think she has answered you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, that was a terrific incident, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which one are you referring to? Would you please explain?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the people were firing the machine gun over your head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I was terrified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, that's the kind of thing that would stick in a person's mind, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I have many problems of my own. I believe that I will remember other things that I forgot to say. Perhaps, this time I didn't say how they brought retarded girls to the camp and all the things they did to them. There was a Croat young woman among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you gave your statement in June of 1994 to the court, to the investigating magistrate in the former Yugoslavia, he asked you questions to find out what had occurred, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe. I really do not remember anything. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you gave your statement to the investigators from the tribunal, they asked you some questions to help you remember things, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe they did. I really have little knowledge of courts and statements. What I could recall at that moment I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were asking questions to help you remember these things, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They can't help me to remember when I know the torment I went through. I know best. I just recounted what I could remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, and you just did not remember about that machine gun until today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably. I don't know. Maybe I did say that, but that is what happened, and I know that is the truth. Now whether I said it or not, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you talked -- in preparation for your testimony here today did you look at any documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to, say, Ms McHenry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who is that? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, that is the woman sitting over there that was asking those questions of you earlier today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not today. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you talk to her in preparing to testify here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know. She doesn't know my language and I don't know hers. Maybe I did, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, I would ask you to look at all four of those people that are silting over at the prosecution bench. Did you talk to any of them in preparation for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall, no, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to anyone from the Office of the Prosecutor about your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I arrived by myself. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So basically you came from wherever you are currently residing to The Hague and then when you came to the court, the tribunal, the first time you talked about what had occurred to you was when you were silting in that witness chair; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. Well, when you came here to testify -- you are no longer residing in Donje Selo I presume,?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you came from wherever you are residing, and I am not asking you where, and you came from there to Holland and you got here some time last week, I guess; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just came -- you did not talk to anybody about your testimony after you have got to the Hague; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know with whom, openly with the women who were there with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What women were there with you, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know these people. There were some interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you talked to them about what you were going to testify to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. No. We just talked what Holland is like, whether we like it or not, what the food was like, what the accommodation was like. I knitted and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one last thing, ma'am, and then I think I shall be done with all of my questions. You testified that you saw a bucket being brought out from tunnel 9 every morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bucket was being brought out where they urinated, I guess, during the night, and then every morning it would be brought out and it would be emptied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It happened every morning that you saw; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see it every morning. Only when I peeked out and see it. I didn't dare look all the time. The last ones when we were coming out always had the bucket with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you peeked out, where did you peek out from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From that room with three windows that were looking out towards the number 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the room where the guards were; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were outside for the most part unless it rained, so that they were not there, so that sometimes I was able to peek out, but I would usually take the jug with me so that if they saw me, it would look as if I was going to get some water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the room where you were held, you could pretty well go in and out of that room any time you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes when we dared -- sometimes they would say that we couldn't look, couldn't watch, and so we didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you could pretty well go in and out of that room whenever you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could, but I often did not dare do it. Sometimes when I would go to the toilet, I would sort of peek out. So we couldn't go in to just watch from that window. It would have to look sort of accidental. I would sometimes peek out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, so the door to the room where you were held was not kept closed, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the door. That door was not locked. Only the outside door was locked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you could come and go from the room you were being held in pretty much whenever you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. Asked and answered. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I do not really see the nature -- because she has explained how she can reach inside and outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: All right, your Honour. Thank you very much. I will withdraw the question. By the way, you said that the food that you were getting was not -- was very small quantities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bad food and small quantities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the guards were eating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the food was cooked at Celebici in the camp or whether it was brought from some place else to the camp to feed the guards and the inmates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know where it was coming from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have just a few seconds? (Pause). Ma'am, were you allowed to have visitors at the reception area of the gate house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Nobody came to visit me. It was not allowed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No-one at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My sister came a number of times to me and my son, but -- and her son, and they wouldn't let her in, Hazim Delic and others, and he bragged that 60 Delic girls and boys will be born because that is how many women he raped. Those were the stories that went around, but I never got a visit. I never knew what happened with my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, let me just ask a couple more things. How did your husband die?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am still not clear about that. I am still unclear about that. At first I thought that he stepped on a mine. I didn't know what the landmines were, and I still am not clear. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But your husband was never a prisoner anywhere, was he, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. He left on August 22nd from Donje Selo. That is what my brother-in-law said, and he hid in and around the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, between May and August 22nd your husband was free, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is no freedom if he was in a cellar. 42 days in a cellar of Trile and it was 80 cms high, this is where they went to the toilet, where they spent all their time. That was no freedom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he was never in the custody of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Until then he was not, because he hid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your two other relatives who were killed about the same time, again they perhaps stepped on landmines or were killed in battle, something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They tried to get out and as soon as they went, they were killed. I don't know if somebody killed them. I don't know, but they were dead. I went to the morgue and I saw them. They certainly did not attack or murder anyone themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they certainly were not inmates of Celebici, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they stayed with my husband and hid with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will pass the witness. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is the end of the cross-examination for the third accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not want to shock you, but we have no questions for this witness. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Nothing shocks me. At least I know how proceedings should go. Any other cross-examination? Cross-examination by MS RESIDOVIC. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, Mrs Cecez, I am Edina Residovic. I am defence counsel for Zejnil Delalic. First, allow me to tell you that I understand that it is not easy for you to answer all our questions. You are on the witness stand for the second day, but I also hope that you understand my own duty and need to ask you questions relating to the events that you have described: I will also try to make my questions simple and clear, and please answer them also in the same manner. Should you not understand the questions or the interpretation, please say so, and I will repeat the question, so that we can understand each other. Do you agree with that, Mrs Cecez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As you stated, you gave your first statement in June to the investigative magistrate in Borci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was then. I don't know what month it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember the year but do you remember it was in Borci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, somebody came to Borci and they asked questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, you did not go to Nevesinje to give this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a statement somebody said you gave a statement in Nevesinje, that would not be true; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the investigators of this tribunal you gave two statements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I came once in December of 1995 and on 14th November 1996."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only came here once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if there are two statements, one would not be yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know that I came here to The Hague once. It was too much travelling for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give a statement in December of 1995 at a different location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In December of 1995 I think it was here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 14th November 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask just two things. One is just to ask that there be a break between defence counsel's questions and the witness's answer just because for us people listening it is going a little too fast. Not only sometimes is it hard to tell what the question and answer is. Certainly it takes away any chance that we might have to object. The second thing is: may I just suggest that the defence counsel show the witness the 2nd November 1996 statement, because I believe that may refresh the recollection and it may have to do with the definition of "statement" and things like that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They speak the same language. Therefore it is going a little more quicker. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): May I show the two statements to the witness? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Well, if you want to, there is nothing wrong in doing that: it's even easier for you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: What language was the statement taken in? Her own language? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I have the statement in the language of the witness. As far as I know, the investigators always took statements in English. Have you seen the statement, Mrs Cecez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This second one is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you explain which one is not clear, as I do not have them here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second one dated November 1996; is that the one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where is the date? 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are not sure that you made that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't even know what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It does not matter what it says. Just answer whether you remember that in November 1996 you spoke to the investigator of the prosecution making an additional statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know when it was. Maybe I did. Maybe I didn't. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question earlier on you said that you had not spoken earlier with Mrs Teresa McHenry, and on this document it says that Mrs McHenry was present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe she was, but I really do not recollect. I do not remember people very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs Cecez, in both cases when the investigator of the tribunal was questioning you or on one occasion, as you remember, you said that you were ready to testify before this tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I spoke the truth. There is absolutely no problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On both occasions or once the investigator was a woman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose so. There was a tall blonde woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs Sabine Manke; is that the one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that just once that you were questioned by her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to The Hague only once. I can't remember anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement that you made in Borci, as you say, and in the statement before Mrs Manke, you did not mention, nor did you have any reason to mention, Mr Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him there, so then I couldn't say anything about him, about something I hadn't seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs Cecez, it is difficult for me to put a question to you, because in the statement which you do not recall having made you obviously in answer to somebody's question mentioned the name of Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were may neighbours, so I knew them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you said that during the course of this morning in your testimony. My question is: if somebody else were not to prompt you to mention him, you had no need to mention Zejnil Delalic in connection with the events you were describing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot cast a suspicion on somebody who did me no evil.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You have answered my question. Allow me to continue. You said that you were born in Ostrozac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your family lived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your father lived in Ostrozac until the end of 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: May I kindly appeal to counsel. The dialogue is getting too fast for everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You see, the interpreter is the same, so the questions and the answers really get muddled up. If you are a little slower, wait for her reply, so we will be able to find out what she is saying and what you are asking, because the interpreter is the same. Getting the same voices in quick succession, it is very difficult to make out what the question is and what the answer is. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. It is obvious that sometimes I forget that, because I speak in the same language as the witness. I will try to speak more slowly. Do you know that the Serbs who lived in Ostrozac the whole time were in good relationships with their neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I couldn't go there. I only went there once to visit my brother when I came out of the camp so I don't know and if they had good relations, surely they wouldn't have left too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that your neighbours, when invited by the authorities in Jablanica, surrendered their arms of their own free will? Thank you. You said yesterday some time in mid-May 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let us have the answer to the last question. They surrendered their weapons. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Peacefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I am not informed about these things. I have no idea. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): And do you know, Mrs Cecez, whether any of them were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your own from Ostrozac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yesterday you said that you went to Konjic for the last time some time in mid-May. You said an exact date I don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19th May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, to bring in your intake from the store. Was the city shelled at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that it was, but I was afraid to go alone. I asked Tidja Zekic, a Muslim woman, to come with me. We had quite a bit of money and I was afraid to go alone. I took it on 19th. I saw people were already in multi-coloured clothes. I was surprised what kind of clothes they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see destroyed houses, stores?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not. Do you know that until 19th Konjic was heavily shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no idea. I don't remember anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, you don't know who shelled it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, Mrs Cecez, as a woman born in Hercegovina, as a citizen of Bosnia-Hercegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born there. I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina. My colleague asked you a little while ago whether it was true that some people were looking in particular for your husband by his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When they got to the house, they shouted out: "Lazar, surrender. We won't hurt you." My house was in the centre of town, of the village. There were buses, cars there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please can you confirm this: did I hear well that two police cars came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one in front and one behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement given to the prosecution you said that your husband jumped out and left, and fled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that earlier he worked in a police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did and he retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to me whether before that day any people were arrested or taken from Donje Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe but I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: People from the police station were people who worked with your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see at the time, but I am sure they did, because they were driving the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs Cecez, is it normal that people flee when they see their colleagues from work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea, but we were living in fear already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to me whether your husband had any reasons to flee when he heard that they were coming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you. Often from the right bank of the Neretva river there was shooting, so we were afraid to go out. So he spent most of his time inside the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Miss Cecez, you were a well-off family in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bjelovcina and Cerici are your neighbouring villages. Do you know the name of Milijan Cecez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in the area of Donje Selo there were barricades erected and checkpoints which blocked free passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know and I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you not know or do you not remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether your husband took part in organising these checkpoints and barricades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember anything at all. I was doing my work in my house, so I don't remember any of that. He liked to go fishing mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your late husband also know Mirjana Cecez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mirjana Cecez left somewhat earlier. He left that area a bit earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that, following that, your husband took over the organisation of arming of Cerici, Donje Selo and Bjelovcina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't remember, nor is that possible. How could he bring weapons?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the future, may I object to the relevancy of what her husband may or may not have done with respect to her testimony and her confinement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: She made a statement they were looking for her husband. She wants to find out why. This cross-examination arises out of a statement she made in direct examination. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think you can carry on. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. Please will you answer my question? Do you know whether your husband, after the departure of Milijan Cecez, took over the duty of arming of the Serbian population in these villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not familiar with any of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If other documents or other witnesses say different, will you say that they do not speak the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will not claim anything for anybody, but what I don't remember, I can't remember, and it's easiest to blame a dead man today for something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs Cecez, when asked by the prosecutor, you said that you knew who Dr Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic is. Can you repeat that now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I know. He was President of the municipality for a time. I don't know for how long. He would come to the camp and I knew him from before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that Dr Rusmir, before these events that you spoke about, together with other representatives of the authorities, tried repeatedly to negotiate the surrender of arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If somebody else comes to and asserts that he will not know this because you don't know the facts; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. Your Honour, I am going to object to asking when she has already said she does not know, so it is improper for her to have an opinion as to what other people may or may not have said. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: These questions have been answered. I do not know why you want to worry yourself about it. If she will not accept whatever they have said, she will say so. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Mrs Cecez, was your late husband a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Jovanka your sister-in-law who worked at the SDS in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of the decision of the SDS on establishment of the Serbian municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea. I really don't understand any of those things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only have two more questions, with apologies for being too long. Can you tell us, do you know that in the fighting for Donje Selo several members of the MUP were also killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean when it was attacked, when Donje Selo was attacked?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time when there was fighting in that area. Nobody was killed until that day, and then I heard that somebody called Velija was killed, and Pavo Mucic told me that somebody called Narcis had killed him from behind. So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just ask you what you know and not what has been told to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I know is Velija was killed and Narcis killed him and Pavo told me Narcis had killed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs Cecez, you recognised your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only by his teeth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are sure that he was not in Celebici and he was not exposed to any torture there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never heard that he was in Celebici, whether they caught him alive and then tortured him. I don't know. The main thing is that he is gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your husband was a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, just like you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course we were. We were born there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement before this tribunal and earlier you spoke about some other persons that you met in Celebici. Ivica Buric, was he a Muslim Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume he was a Croat. They called him Ivica Buric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that a certain Zvonimir also came in with the MUP to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he also a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Croat and he is married to a Serbian woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in Celebici did you see members of the military police or the HVO there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know really. I don't understand these signs, but anyway there was told us that the Croats were terrible people, that we shouldn't have any contact with them and as soon as we saw the insignia on their sleeves, I would hide from the window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was going to finish, but I have an additional question, so please indulge me. I would like to ask it, to put it to Mrs Cecez. Do you know whether a commission was working in Celebici questioning prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I was questioned only once, for a short time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had no opportunity to see where they were questioning people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, given in 1994, you stated that your physician gave you a prescription for pills that my colleague questioned you about. Did you speak the truth then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The doctor had prescribed them before, because I used them for five, six, seven years. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But specifically the pills in this case, were they prescribed by a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I always had that prescription in reserve, so I'd go to the pharmacy and I'd buy them. So I kept using the same pills. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I thought she said that several times. This has been repeated that she had these pills since 1986 and now she wants to buy new ones. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I only wanted it entered into the transcript. Thank you. However, today she said that she bought them without a prescription, so we wanted to clarify that point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They can be purchased without a prescription, because it is a private pharmacy. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, Mrs Cecez. Thank you, your Honours. I have no more questions. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Mr Tapuskovic, any questions? MR TAPUSKOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, on behalf of the team defending Mr Mucic the questions will be put by Mr Mike Greaves. I would just like for an explanation concerning me. I deserved your objections, but I appeal to you to have some understanding for us lawyers coming from these parts. In my country I do not get permission to speak. I just get up and wait for permission. So please forgive me for this error. It was not at all my intention to insult the court. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: There is no reason why you should be too worried. All I objected to was two people speaking at the same time. It is not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Will your Honour just give me a moment? Cross-examination by MR GREAVES.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The scale was 1:12,000. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe it was 1:50,000, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I am just wondering if this is the map of Donje Selo. Let us find out. Donje Selo. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Well, Mr Greaves. Thank you very much. Let me just give you have a short warning. We might break at 4 to reassemble about 4.20, 4.25, although you will continue cross-examining when you come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I wonder if you prefer I do it now in one go. Perhaps you might like to rise now for the same period. Would that be a sensible way of doing it rather than my breaking off halfway? I would prefer it if you -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Then we will break now and come back at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that is very helpful. (3.55 pm) (Short break) (4.17 pm) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Please call the witness; she is still on her oath. Mr Greaves, your witness. Cross-examined by MR GREAVES

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May it please your Honour. Mrs Cecez, I would like to ask you one or two questions to start with about your escape, if I may call it that, to Serb territory in November 1992. That would be about two months after your release from Celebici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I answer this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I did ask a question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question was not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry. Please tell me if you do not understand the question. Your escape from Donje Selo to Serb territory, that was in November 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 11th November 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The distance you had to travel that day, was that about 5 kms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was much more, because I started from Donje Selo and ended up in Hadici near Kobilica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is that that you had to travel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it all by road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly macadam roomed. Sometimes we would have a part that had asphalt on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Instead of distance, perhaps you can tell us how long the journey took? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is in terms of time, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In terms of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not looking at a watch. I wasn't watching it, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can tell us what time of day was it that you set off? Was it in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, early in the morning. I don't recall the exact time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it still dark when you left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It had become daylight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of day did you arrive eventually in Serb-held territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived some time maybe 4, 4.30. I don't know but it was close to dusk, because we met a man when we arrived and I don't know where this man was from and the people who had brought us departed and he took us with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a Serbian man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not the only person who escaped that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We were 7 altogether in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that 7 women or men and women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 6 women and one young man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall who exactly went with you that day, what their names were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't recall. I only know that they were Croats and apparently they were in the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No-one else from your village escaped that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe there were. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs Cecez, is it right that the person who paid for your journey, that was Pavo Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure, but I imagine that it was him who paid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the sum was 300 German Marks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time they were asking 300 Marks from our people, and I thought that is what they were asking of us, and we didn't pay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't pay it; someone else did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the arrangements were made by Mr Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from Mr Mucic, there was a Croat driver, who drove the vehicle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those two Croats that were with us, they drove and Pavo stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The arrangements that were made put Mr Mucic into danger; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was dangerous to help people escape in this way, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the way did you pass through a number of checkpoints, military checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Somewhere above Butravic Pola there was one checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were many questions asked at those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The driver got out and he spoke to them. We did not get out and we didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now, please, about the period between your release from Celebici and your escape. Did you spend the whole time in Donje Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were able to move about freely within the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because when I went to visit my old house I would always take a child with me, so that people would not shoot if they saw me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you also have a piece of paper, a certificate, which had been given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after I was released from prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A permit to move about freely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was Pavo Mucic wrote it for me for Donje Selo, and I asked him for a certificate to go to Konjic if I had to visit a doctor and also then later I asked him for Ostrozac as well, because my father was 80 years old, and I wanted to be able to visit him as well and he did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he gave up the permission to go to these places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He just wrote it and I went there with another Croat, and nobody saw us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs Cecez, you were not the only woman who was released from Celebici and who went to Donje Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milojka was also released with me but she went to Pokojiste and I went to Donje Selo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was she released on the same day as you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other women who had been released at different times from the same camp in Donje Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who was detained, because I found no women from Donje Selo there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were there some who returned to Donje Selo at about the same time as you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I was the longest there. I was one of the first that was detained and that stayed there the longest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pavo Mucic came to visit you when you were -- after your release, came to visit you in the village, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he visited you several times, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On those occasions when he visited you he gave food and things like that to you, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did once, some food. Had they not burned the house down, I would have had enough food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you plainly needed food, and that is what he gave to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did deliver food once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to suggest to you that it was more than once, Mrs Cecez, and that your memory may be at fault after five years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was only once that he delivered it to me, but he may have delivered it several times to others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard that he had done that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I guess people talked about that. My brother-in-law said that he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly on one of the visits that he made to you there was a conversation that you had with him about what had happened in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with this, that he was surprised at what you told him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He looked at if he was surprised, as if he didn't know anything, but I doubt that he didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I am going to ask you this. When you told him, he was not only surprised, but he was also distressed, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He said: "Why did you not ask for me?" I said that I did but he was not coming. I said either the guards did not tell him or he didn't want to come. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you could see his reaction was one of surprise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is simply -- I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. He said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is only your opinion that he may not have been surprised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my opinion, but then maybe the man didn't know about anything. I don't know but he should have known. He should have visited us while we were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He also spoke to you about the girl of 13?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And told you that he tried to stop whatever was going to happen to her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now, please, about your actual release from Celebici camp on 31st August 1992. Do you recall that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall that day. It was a Monday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs Cecez, I am going to ask the court to show you a short piece of videotape, which comes from prosecution exhibit M1?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has not yet been exhibited. If the defence wishes to enter it in evidence, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am very grateful. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes, you can go ahead with that. You can now tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As a defence exhibit. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the video is not playing on her screen. She is the important one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I clarify for the record this is tape M1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It is tape M1. I think within M1 there are four exhibits, A, B, C, D. We are not sure whether it is A, B, C or D. We cannot identify it from the notation on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: We will clarify that later for the court so the court is clear what is entered into evidence. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Let us get her the actual exhibit you want, the picture you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would your Honour just give me a moment, please? (Video presentation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs Cecez, you've got the picture now, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just of one man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want you to look at, please, is the men in the pictures that you see, and I would like you to think about who they might be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see this man but I can't remember who he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I would like you just to look at the film and then at the end of the film, if there are people who you recognise in the film, I would like you to tell us who they are, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the brother of my sister -- no, no, the father of my sister-in-law, Milijan, Milijan Djordjic from Bradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the man on the right in the blue cap?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this one. This is Milijan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man in the yellow jersey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one. Her father, as far as I can see, Milijan Djordjic, an elderly man from Bradina. I think that is him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the men in the background that we can see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't see who they are. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: There is not just one man. There is more than one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There are five faces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I don't know them but this one I know. He is a friend of mine and I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was there anybody else that you recognised in that short bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to turn now, please, to some of the accounts that you have given in connection with these proceedings, Mrs Cecez. Can you recall, please, the occasion in June 1994 when you were summoned to a court and asked questions about these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at, please, a document and ask you to identify your signature, please? Mrs Cecez, take your time, if you need to, but just look at that document and see if you can see your signature at the bottom of each page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you just read the top part of the first page, please? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The document is not in evidence yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am just asking her to refresh her memory, if she would, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you exhibiting it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am not exhibiting it at this moment. Thank you very much. I just want to ask her to refresh her memory about her signature and where it was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I suggest you bring the document up and refer it, if you plan it to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my signature but I don't know how is it possible it is in Nevesinje. Maybe these people who took down these notes put "Nevesinje" on top.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I just want to establish that it is her signature, your Honour. Thank you very much, Mrs Cecez. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It does not appear to go to any issue at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No. We will come to it in a moment, if we may, please. Thank you very much, Mrs Cecez. You do not need to look at that at the moment. You think it was somewhere else that you attended that day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the day, but I didn't make any statements in Nevesinje, as far as I can remember. Only in Borci. Maybe those people by omission put Nevesinje. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is perfectly possible. It may not matter where it was. But in any event do you recall answering questions about two and a half years ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If they asked me, I probably answered, as far as I could remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you were asked the questions, do you recall this: you were warned of the obligation to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And warned of the obligation not to suppress facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not conceal facts. I tell the truth always, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were reminded of that on that occasion, were you not, your duty to do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must object. This has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I do not think he has answered the question. She says: "I do not." The learned counsel is asking her whether she was reminded of her obligation. That is a different question and different answer from the one "I always speak the truth."

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. I will ask the question again. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually the contention again is a different one. She does not even remember making any statement at that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right. In fact, she has answered that and perhaps I am being excessive in going through it in such detail and I ask your forgiveness. In any event you signed on those pages, Mrs Cecez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you accept from me that in that account that you gave you told that court while you were in the camp Pavo Mucic did not visit, and I only saw him a few times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't enter our room. Only on one occasion with a little girl he came in and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you that you only saw him a few times, because he only arrived at the camp in early August 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is there a question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was there the first evening. The first evening he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mrs Cecez, what I want to ask you is this: he was not there on the first evening, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as I arrived, he came on that same evening, on 27th May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the account that you gave in 1994 you did not mention that Pavo Mucic was there on the night that you arrived at Celebici camp, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was there. I am sure of that. He was there. Maybe I left it out. I don't know exactly what I said, but I am sure he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is only since 1994 that you have said that he was there on that first night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I always claim that he was there and he was there. I am sure of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no mention at any time of the incident involving the machine gun?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is that a question, your Honour? I must object to this form of examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think it is a question, yes. Thank you very much. At no time I suggest to you did you ever say to anybody any incident concerning the machine gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe at that moment I didn't remember it, but whenever I met with people, with my children, I spoke about it, but maybe on that particular occasion I left it out. I claim that that was what happened. He was there and he fired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you that that incident never happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did happen. It did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly Pavo Mucic never took part in any such incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did. I saw him with my own eyes, and no-one can persuade me otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I suggest to you is that you saw more of him after your release than you did at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I saw him in camp more often than when I was released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us about this: do you know the man called Tarzan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Is that the end of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The witness can now stand down. Except you have any other things for her, she should be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for listening to me with attention. I am very grateful to you. Thank you and goodbye. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. (Witness withdrew) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Any other witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we have our next witness, the expert witness of the prosecution. However, it is soon 5 o'clock and it is the wish of the expert witness to start afresh tomorrow and give her statement in one turn. I just bring that to you, but we are in principle ready. MR KARIBI WHYTE: Is the witness around?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The witness is around, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think ideally she can start tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Then I wish to call Dr Calic as my next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: In the meantime, your Honour, I can inform the Trial Chamber about Mr Rod Dixon who is helping us with the paper supporting our expert witness with exhibits and things. DR MARIE-JANINE CALIC (sworn) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Okay. You can sit down. Take a seat. Examined by MR OSTBERG

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Are you ready?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am ready.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. At least you have 35 minutes of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please state to the court your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Marie-Janine Calic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the defence lawyers tried to question your objectivity at this time because of your name. Does it have a Slav or Serbian ring to it, your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my father's name and my father is born in Istria, which today is a part of Croatia, but he left the country before the Second World War. My mother is German. I was born in Germany and brought up there and I am a German citizen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any ties to any of the parties to the Yugoslav conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have no ties. I have a lot of professional contacts in several republics of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you belong to any religions of these parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I belong to no religion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: None at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you consider yourself an unbiased and objective scholar in the field of your expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell the court about your present occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am working in a research institute for international affairs. This is a kind of a German think-tank. It is of a private foundation, but it is financed by the federal budget of Germany. We are supposed to provide the German ministries and the German Parliament with analysis in the field of international affairs. I am there the person who is concentrated on South-eastern Europe. I have been working there since 1992, and I mainly concentrated on the area of the former Yugoslavia.
