utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many scholars or academics are working in this institute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About fifty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fifty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have in a binder, which I will -- which already has been presented to the defence, and which I would like to also bring to the court. It consists of 58 documents, which I intend to offer or tender as evidence when I have finished my examination of Dr Calic, who is going to rely on many of these documents during her presentation. They are, as far as I know, not yet marked for identification, and I think maybe that can also wait until they are tendered. We have three binders for the members of the court? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: These documents have been prepared by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: These documents have been prepared by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. The first document, Dr Calic, in this binder is your curriculum vitae. I am not going to go through it with you. I would just like to ask you a few things about it. What is the title of your doctoral thesis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The title is "The Social History of Serbia in the 19th and First Half of the 20th Centuries".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many works including books and major articles have you published in this field of your expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About fifty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first one and when was the last one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first one was, if I recall well, in 1985 and the last one recently, very recently, a few weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is over a period of 12 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you get your doctorate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got it in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were invited by the Office of the Prosecutor to appear before this Trial Chamber as an expert witness in this trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you go about preparing your statement to give to this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I relied mostly on documents and research which I have done before during my professional experience in this field, and I was also given some documents by the Office of the Prosecution. They included also documents coming from the defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you start to prepare for this expert statement you are supposed to give to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started to prepare by the end of last year, in December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have just seen to it that you have been served with this binder with these documents in. I have agreed with Dr Calic to go through her statement as it appears in the written report and then, when passing through it, have Dr Calic present these documents on which she relies to us. May I now ask you, Dr Calic, to start your statement by giving us a background to the conflict and start by telling us something about the main political and military developments and structures in Bosnia-Herzegovina after 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I start right now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. Let me say first this report I have done is based mostly on my personal research, but I also rely on experts in this field. I used documents coming from the former Yugoslavia. I used reports from international organisations, and, as I was saying before, I also used some documents made available to me by the Office of the Prosecutor. I have concentrated in this report on certain questions, so I also would like to stress that this is not a comprehensive report on everything that was going on in the former Yugoslavia, but I have chosen certain areas, and these areas are the main political and military developments and structures in Bosnia and Herzegovina after 1990. In the second part I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe, Dr Calic, you should not speak so fast, because we have a translations problem here, and then it is also heavy stuff you are bringing us, so please try to speak not too fast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I then would like to concentrate on the main military forces in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992. I go through the main political, military and legal functions of the Yugoslav municipalities. I am going through the main characteristics of the municipality of Konjic, and I also try to reconstruct the main developments, political and military developments, in the Konjic municipality in 1992. Before I start with my first part, I would like to present a map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is document number 2 in this binder, and document number 2 is the map of Jugoslavia before the war. Should I put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We have nothing in the computer system, so I think you should put these things on the ELMO. Could somebody assist Dr Calic with some light there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I go on? The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia comprised of six republics, Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see you, Dr Calic, but we don't see the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see the model.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Could we arrange it so we can see even the map on our screens? I don't know how this works, or do we just look upon it in our -- somebody is coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Does it work now? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Is this map available to the defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, the defence has the same. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think it is now appearing on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might suggest, the prosecution did provide all of us with the notebooks, as you have on your desk, but because we did not take a break between witnesses our notebooks are in the defence room. We would probably be more at an advantage if we had our notebooks in front of us so we could follow along also, but they are in the defence room as we speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: These things we are talking about -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: This is not a difficult aspect of it. That is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What we have for the moment is the map. I think you can proceed. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It is simple. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, we have only part of the map of Yugoslavia,. Slovenia and Macedonia cannot be seen. Could we please have a map of the whole SFRY? It is only one. This one has a different name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: It has to be moved and we can see all of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It can be moved. Like this you see Slovenia and like this you see Macedonia. I think it is a technical problem. It is not a problem of the map. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): It is a technical problem but it is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Now you see all of it. Please, Dr Calic. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: You carry on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I continue? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Six republics, with the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the middle. The Federation embraced the complex mix of ethnic groups and no single group was wholly contained within any republic. Bosnia: many people believe that Bosnia was the heart of Yugoslavia not only because it was in the middle but also it had the form of a heart and also because of its ethnic composition. Let me put briefly document number 3, a map of the ethnic composition of Yugoslavia in 1991, and I hope we will not have the same problem with the screen. No, we don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: There we are. We see it all. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All together there were about 20 nations and nationalities living in Yugoslavia and also in Bosnia were living 20 nations and nationalities. For political, constitutional and social and economic reasons Yugoslavia started to dissolve at the end of the 1980s. On 25th June 1991 Slovenia and Croatia declared their independence. Serbia and Montenegro on the other hand, as well as many Serbs living in Croatia and in Serbia and in Bosnia claimed they wished to preserve Yugoslavia. Immediately after the declaration of independence the first armed conflicts erupted between the newly-created armed forces of Slovenia and Croatia on the one side, and the federal and the Serb armed forces on the other side. In the light of these events the general situation in Bosnia started to deteriorate very rapidly. According to the 1991 census Bosnia and Herzegovina's population of 4.4 million was composed of 43 per cent Muslims; 31 per cent Serbs; and 17 per cent Croats. Many parts of this country were ethnically mixed. We have to illustrate this fact a fourth document, document number 4. Bosnia, because of this fact, was called a little Yugoslavia. Bosnians often claimed that it was exactly the other way round, that Yugoslavia was, in fact, a big Bosnia. In the first multi-party elections of November 1990 in Bosnia and Herzegovina the three national-oriented parties, SDA, the Muslim-dominated party of Democratic Action; the SDS, the Serb-dominated party; and the HDZ, the Croat- dominated party, got the majority of the seats in the National Assembly. There were altogether 41 parties --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honours. I believe she refers to a document number 4 that we do not have on our screen or anything that she is testifying from. Is there a document number 4 that we are supposed to be seeing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the population census of Bosnia in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can that be -- is it possible to show it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: If it can be read there. I don't know if it is possible to enlarge it. Yes, it is indeed. That was a bit too much really.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You actually wanted to see the population census?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We just wanted to know what you were testifying from, because we had no evidence of it. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually you do not really need what she was testifying from.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe we do. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: She need not produce this if she can tell it. She is testifying as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you in understandable terms summarise it to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I just did. It is the population figures for Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991 from the official Bosnian census, and what I wanted to say is that the population of 40.3 million people was composed of about 43 per cent Muslims, 31 per cent Serbs and 17 per cent Croats. There were, of course, many other nations and nationalities. We can see them also from the same document. This is all what I wanted to say with this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under the headline "Total"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We cannot read the numbers. Can we move this on the screen to the margin so we can see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which numbers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The composition of it? If you start from -- just to help the defence -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I do not know why we are wasting time on a matter of public record. These are records which can be got anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I want to find out what does the word "Hrvati" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is writing at the top of this document number 4, "Hrvati". Under that is "Musilmani"; then "Serbi".

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How do you pronounce it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hrvati.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Hrvati. So I can write down, it is really Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already mentioned the first elections of November 1990. 41 parties, but only five of them were bigger parties, and the three national-oriented parties. This is again -- yes, it has to be reduced -- of SDA, HDZ and SDS got the majority of the votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Could you clarify for us -- I think we all understand with these green, red and blue sectors of this circle, but if we go to the SKSDP and SRSJ and others, would you please expand on that a bit, so we can understand what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. The SKSDP is the League of Communists, a former communist party. The SRSJ is the Alliance of Reformed Forces. The two parties were Yugoslav-oriented ethnically mixed, explicitly ethnically mixed parties, but they were defeated in these elections, and, as I was saying before, the majority of seats going to the three national-oriented parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What was the total number of seats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What was the total number of seats?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: In the black sector there were how many others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 35 other parties, but they got so few votes that it is not even worth mentioning them. They were a regional-based parties and others. So 35. The important thing is that the election results more or less reflected the ethnic composition of Bosnia's population and that the three big parties agreed to form a coalition government. Each of them was represented in the seven-member presidency of the Bosnian state. The Muslim Alija Izetbegovic became President of the Republican Presidency; the Serb politician Krajisnik was appointed President of the National Assembly; and the Croat Pelivan was chosen to be the Prime Minister. The three national parties, however, became very soon after the elections deadlocked over two very important questions. The first question concerned the political status of Bosnia. Should Yugoslavia be dissolved, so the question was: should Bosnia also become independent? Should other republics cede from Yugoslavia or should Yugoslavia be dissolved? The second important question was: how should the multi-ethnic Republic of Bosnia be structured constitutionally then? Should it be a centralised state or should it be a federal state? So the two questions, political status and future constitutional set-up, were discussed, and actually the parties became then deadlocked over these two questions. As far as the first question, the question of the constitution, the Serbs and later on also the Croat leadership, who had in mind the unification of their national with their mother countries, they proposed the cantonisation of Bosnia into three or more ethnically defined regions. Many were talking about the Swiss model at that time. Cantonisation was on the agenda. The Muslim leadership, on the other hand, sought to preserve Bosnia as a unified, multi-ethnic and as a unitarian state. This had, of course, several reasons. One reason was the way how the people of Yugoslavia settled. Muslims were concentrated in towns, and for them it would have been much more difficult to carve out cantons, ethnically defined cantons than, for example, for the Croats, who were settling more compact near the border of Croatia, but, of course, also Serbs and Croats were somehow scattered across Bosnia. There were also many mixed marriages and many mixed families, so this was another problem, and there was also the danger that the state of Bosnia would soon split up once the constitution was based on ethnic criteria. The debate over how to reconstruct the Republic of Bosnia created a constitutional and also legal vacuum in 1991, and together with the war in Croatia it accelerated the difficulties of Bosnian society along ethnic lines. All three parties placed greater emphasis on ethnic criteria in public life and step by step ethnic polarisation occurred nearly everywhere in the Bosnian society, in the media, public life, education system and also in the security forces, but I will come back to this problem later. In this context the question of whether Bosnia should become independent or not had arisen. Croatia and Slovenia in late 1990 had proposed to transform Yugoslavia into a confederation of quasi-independent states with very big, weak common confederal institutions. Serbia had opposed this plan while Bosnia and Macedonia presented a compromise plan. This was in June 1991 and this plan was rejected by the other parties. After the outbreak of war in Croatia in the summer of 1991 the SDA and also the HDZ started to favour independence. The Bosnian Serb leadership, on the other hand, was against independence, and they had already taken steps towards forming autonomous areas with quasi-state powers, and they declared in September 1991 some of these areas as Serbian autonomous areas. The crisis came to a head in October 1991, when the Croat and the Muslim members of the Parliament declared Bosnia's sovereignty -- this was on 14th October 1991 -- while the Serb representatives had declared their opposition to independence. To illustrate this debate over the future of Bosnia I included in the file a document number 6 by the European Commission. It is Opinion Number 1 of the European Commission's Arbitration Commission. Can we see it on the screen? Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the heading number "137"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Opinion Number 1 of the Arbitration Commission on the Peace Conference on Yugoslavia. The peace conference was established in September 1991 and they also formed this Arbitration Commission under the French constitutional expert Badinter, so this is the Opinion Number 1 of the so-called Badinter Commission. I don't know if you can read it either on the document or on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it is readable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know it is readable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me it is. Is it for you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is on the screen, I suppose, readable for these who do not have the document in their hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is in here also.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: It is in the binder, but I think people who do not have the binder, because it is elsewhere in the building, can read it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the European Union's Communities at this time -- the European Union's Arbitration Commission recognised that there was a very serious debate over major legal questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. Arbitration Commission. An arbitration needs a prior agreement to refer a matter to arbitration. Who appointed the Arbitration Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The European Commission established in September 1991 peace conference. The idea of this peace conference was to mediate between the parties to the conflict, that is to say between the leaderships of the former republics, and there were quite a lot of activities going on within this conference, and one of the activities was the creation of this Arbitration Commission, and they formulated a number of opinions. This is the first. I come later back to another opinion of this Arbitration Commission to illustrate a different event. This is to show and to -- yes, to show how serious and how concerned also the international community was about what was going on in the former Yugoslavia. It says: "Serbia considers that those republics which have declared or would declare themselves independent of sovereignty have seceded or would secede from the SFRY, which would otherwise continue to exist. Other republics on the country consider that there is no question of cessation, but the question is one of disintegration or breaking up of the SFRY as the result of the concurring work of a number of republics". This is the very --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt? The question from Judge Jan, who said: 'Who set up this Arbitration Committee?', was this formed by this conference which was convened on Yugoslavia here in The Hague, if I remember correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This conference made a decision to set up an Arbitration Committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big was that Arbitration Committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Five members. That had the name of Badinter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name was correctly Arbitration Committee -- Arbitration Commission -- I am sorry -- of the Peace Conference on Yugoslavia, but it is known under the name of Badinter. If you refer to Badinter Commission, then more people will understand than if you refer to the Arbitration Commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So this is the very essence of how the conflict started or what the conflict was about, two very different opinions between the republics of the former Yugoslavia on how the future of Yugoslavia should look like. The Serbs continued to contest the legitimacy of the sovereignty declaration of the Muslim and Croat members of the Parliament. They left not only the Bosnian Parliament in October 1991 but also other state institutions, and they created their own Parliament and Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On 24th October 1991 they took a decision for the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina to remain in the common state of Yugoslavia, and this is my document number 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is no translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: There is a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 7. Document number 8 immediately relates to --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Under number 7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 7. So the decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The last page. Yes, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- decision to remain in the Joint Federal State of Yugoslavia. The same day the Serbs took also the decision to create a kind of official representation, a kind of government. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think we might rise now and you will continue tomorrow morning --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: -- at 10.30 tomorrow morning. I think it might be better the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just as a question of order ask the Chamber to agree to have these documents marked as Prosecution Exhibits 6-63 for further entering as evidence. Just do the marking of them, so we have track of them. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: We will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: 6-63. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The Trial Chamber will now rise and resume tomorrow at 10.30.
